source_text: So, regarding the "live incident" I think I have resolved it with some firm words to codex-18 and codex-19, but there's still a bit left over, i.e., if I use start-codex-autorunner I think we should *turn off* transcription of my turns as a result, because they will just be the same time after time until I run stop-codex-autorunner.  That said, if we had a better Cook Ting / Joints processing system, I might not need to use the autorunner at all because we'd have the system design set up in advance.  You could read the "joe:" lines in the codex-19 REPL to get the flavour.  I have given it clear instructions and now intend to say "ok please continue" until they are done.  Last night I figured out an additional level to this which is to say "ok, please continue until we reach the stopping condition at which point run stop-codex-autorunner in your REPL to signal completion".  But all of this seems very "by hand" in comparison to a well-working token-tracking machine that would manage the whole thing for me.

reply_text:
㊥ (autorunner) Done: while the Codex autorunner is armed, its repeated prompt is recorded but never sent to 象 for reading (`bf84b8d9`, loaded in your Emacs). It turns itself back on: as soon as you stop the autorunner, or type anything other than its prompt, your turns are read again. Your last turn also confirmed the frame at RET: 313 appeared as "小象, provisional" straight after you sent it.

㊬ (autorunner, checked) A new test checks three cases:
- the autorunner's prompt is not read;
- your own words in the same buffer still are;
- after stopping, the same prompt is read again.

Such turns are recorded as "not requested", the same as under `象-off`. So they never reach futon1b or a 象 seat.

🈖 (what your codex-19 turns show) I read your `joe:` lines in codex-19. Taken together, they set up everything the machine needs, written out by hand:
- **An owner and a critical path.** The 110 curriculum in Lisp is codex-19's.
- **Routing rules for side work.** Python-to-Lisp bugs go to codex-18, Lean-to-Python bugs to claude-4.
- **A rule against waiting.** "You will not wait for them", and codex-19 works around the bug instead.
- **A progress measure.** `progress.py`, one row at a time.
- **A stopping condition.** Last night's "until we reach the stopping condition, then run stop-codex-autorunner".

Your "ok, please continue" is the machine's nudge, sent by hand.

㊩ (a flaw in our design) My token design gets the no-waiting rule wrong. The stall check (W2) skips an agent whose order has an open child. So if codex-19 sends codex-18 a bug report and then sits idle, it is never nudged. That's exactly the "sitting there waiting for codex-20" that was driving you nuts. Your rule gives the fix: an agent counts as waiting only if it has *declared* that it's waiting by parking on the child's job. An open child alone doesn't excuse it. A bug report is then a child that doesn't block, and an idle codex-19 with no park still holds the token and gets nudged. It's a small change to the pure check, and I'll make it myself when I review W3.

㊭ (replacing the autorunner) A root order could carry the stopping condition as a check the machine computes, not one the agent reports. For example, "`progress.py` shows rows 1–N passing" or "the blank-file target loads". At each job end the machine runs the check:
- **Met:** it closes the root and tells you.
- **Not met, and the agent idle without a park:** it nudges the agent with "continue", plus what the check says is still missing.

That takes over three jobs: your "ok, please continue", the autorunner, and the "run stop-codex-autorunner when done" step. You would set the order up once, with the owner, routing, no-waiting rule and stopping check, and not repeat it by hand.

🈸 (one decision) Shall I add that as W4, root orders with a computed stopping check, once W3 is in? It needs the actual check command for codex-19's curriculum. I'd take that from `progress.py`, if you can say which rows count as done.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (Fong per turn) Yes, I think it can run live and classically, and fast: gluing a pattern to its cascade neighbour and asking a counterfactual took 6 ms just now. The pilot authored its theories by hand from one incident. Per turn, each pattern becomes the same small theory with two pattern-specific parts: a classical test for its IF and its THEN over the turn's acts from 大象. Writing those two tests for each pattern is the real work. Gluing and the logic come almost for free.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text:
(the encoding) A flexiarg already has the shape of an open theory:
- **IF** is an observable: did this turn contain the situation? For wr-26 (the card in your bar): an act switching a capability off.
- **THEN** is an observable: did the turn contain the act the pattern asks for? For wr-26: a re-arm condition with a number in it, in the same turn.
- **HOWEVER** is the failure mechanism: `stranded-flag = switched-off and not rearm-written`.
- **BECAUSE** links to the cost, and that's where the cascade comes in. wr-26's `@why` names `r20-interoceptive-tripwires`. Gluing the two along `stranded-flag` gives `surprise-later`.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (spike, just run) I built wr-26 and r20 that way with the pilot's `open_theory.clj`. They glued. With the evidence "switched off, no re-arm written, surprise later", I asked the counterfactual "had the re-arm been written?" The answer was no surprise, computed deterministically in 6 ms. One limit: the equation grammar is binary, so `not` needs its own intermediate variable. That's harmless.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text:
(what per turn would compute) This would run after 大象 has produced the turn's acts, for the card in the bar plus the patterns 象 cited:
1. **Applies?** IF is true for this turn.
2. **Satisfied?** THEN is true. If not, that's a violation, and the glued cascade says what it leads to downstream. That's a counterfactual you could read in the HUD: "had you done THEN, r20's surprise would not follow."
3. **Unknown.** An IF or THEN with no classical test yet is shown as an open port, not guessed. Your earlier point about stale cards fits here: a card whose IF hasn't applied for several turns is a rule no longer in force.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (the bottleneck) Each pattern needs its two tests written in terms of act kinds plus text cues, such as "a :withdraw on a capability" or "a number in a :constrain". That's a one-off authoring job per pattern. An LLM can draft it offline, it gets reviewed and stored next to the flexiarg, and from then on the per-turn path has no LLM in it. We wouldn't need all 1,227 patterns: the cards that actually get selected into seats are a few dozen. A pattern without tests stays an open port, which is the honest default.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (one decision) The Kimis are all busy. Shall I build the core myself, since it's logic design and I hold the context? It would be: flexiarg → skeleton theory, gluing along `@why`, the per-turn evaluation over the adapter's acts, and IF/THEN tests for the war-room cards. I'd check it against tonight's turns, starting with whether the `象-off` turn applied wr-26 and satisfied it.
